name: LMNA laminopathy with dilated cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy

clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in LMNA, which encodes the nuclear envelope proteins lamin A and C; the same gene underlies a spectrum including dilated cardiomyopathy, Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy and limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 1B

The neuromuscular phenotype often features humeroperoneal or limb-girdle weakness with early, prominent joint contractures (elbows, Achilles tendons and spine) and rigid spine, sometimes preceding overt cardiac symptoms
Cardiac disease characteristically begins with conduction-system involvement, such as atrioventricular block and atrial arrhythmias, and progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure
LMNA cardiolaminopathy carries a high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, which can occur even before or out of proportion to left ventricular dysfunction

Because of this arrhythmic risk, guidelines set a lower threshold for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement rather than a pacemaker alone, taking account of risk markers such as non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, atrioventricular conduction delay, non-missense variants and male sex
Lifelong cardiac surveillance with ECG, ambulatory monitoring and cardiac imaging (echocardiography and cardiac MRI) is essential, and competitive or intense exertion is generally discouraged
There is no cure; management is multidisciplinary and supportive, combining heart failure and device therapy, contracture and respiratory care, and cascade genetic screening of relatives
reference.pathophysiology: LMNA encodes lamins A and C, intermediate filament proteins that form the nuclear lamina underlying the inner nuclear membrane. This meshwork provides mechanical support to the nucleus, organises chromatin and regulates gene expression and mechanotransduction. Pathogenic variants weaken the lamina and disturb these functions, rendering mechanically stressed tissues such as cardiac and skeletal muscle particularly vulnerable. In the heart this produces fibrosis and disease of the conduction system and myocardium, leading to arrhythmia, conduction block and dilated cardiomyopathy, while skeletal muscle involvement causes weakness and the early contractures characteristic of the Emery-Dreifuss and limb-girdle phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy from EMD (emerin) and other genes
Other genetic dilated cardiomyopathies with conduction disease (including desmin and SCN5A)
Myotonic dystrophy with cardiac conduction involvement
Sarcoglycanopathies and other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies
Cardiac sarcoidosis or other infiltrative conduction-system disease
additionalInvestigations: LMNA sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, often within a cardiomyopathy or muscular dystrophy gene panel
12-lead ECG and ambulatory (Holter) monitoring to detect conduction disease and ventricular arrhythmia
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess ventricular function and myocardial fibrosis
Serum creatine kinase, electromyography and, where needed, muscle biopsy for the neuromuscular phenotype
Baseline and serial respiratory function testing given diaphragmatic and spinal involvement
Arrhythmic risk stratification to guide the timing of defibrillator implantation
Cascade genetic testing and cardiac screening of at-risk relatives
redFlags: Syncope, presyncope or documented non-sustained ventricular tachycardia signalling high arrhythmic risk
High-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia
Rapidly declining left ventricular function or decompensated heart failure
Family history of sudden cardiac death in a gene-positive relative
reference.prognosis: Prognosis in LMNA disease is dominated by the cardiac phenotype: conduction disease and dilated cardiomyopathy tend to progress, and the substantial risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death makes early defibrillator protection central to reducing mortality. With timely device therapy, heart failure management and cardiac surveillance, outcomes can be improved, though the neuromuscular component contributes to cumulative disability.
pitfalls: Implanting a pacemaker alone for conduction disease when a defibrillator is warranted because of the sudden-death risk
Underestimating arrhythmic risk in patients with preserved or only mildly reduced ejection fraction
Focusing on the neuromuscular weakness and under-recognising the life-threatening cardiac involvement
Failing to arrange cascade screening, leaving at-risk relatives unprotected
Permitting intense or competitive exercise despite the arrhythmic risk
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Treat the dilated cardiomyopathy with guideline-directed heart failure therapy including ACE inhibitors or an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, beta-blockers and mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists
Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator at a low threshold, rather than a pacemaker alone, because of the high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death
Manage conduction disease and atrial arrhythmias, with anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation as appropriate
Maintain lifelong cardiac surveillance with ECG, ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography and cardiac MRI, and perform arrhythmic risk stratification
Address the neuromuscular phenotype with physiotherapy for contractures, orthoses and monitoring and support of respiratory function including non-invasive ventilation
Advise against competitive or intense exertion given the arrhythmic risk
Refer for advanced heart failure therapies such as mechanical circulatory support or transplantation when indicated
Provide genetic counselling and cascade cardiac and genetic screening of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
